0.0.n: Sets the time frame for the skin changes described next.

0.1.n: Combines with に to describe how abruptly the change began.

0.2.n: Turns 急 into a description of how the change happened.

0.3.n: A casual, friendly word for 頬, often used in everyday conversation.

0.4.n: Links the cheeks to ところ, identifying the area being discussed.

0.5.n: Refers to a part of the face rather than a separate location.

0.6.n: Marks the cheek area as what has started becoming irritated.

0.7.n: Refers to face masks worn over the nose and mouth.

0.8.n: Lists masks as one example, with makeup mentioned next.

1.0.n: Combines with 荒れ to describe skin irritation associated with cosmetics.

1.1.n: The noun form related to 荒れる, used with 化粧 and する to describe irritated skin.

1.2.n: Makes 化粧荒れ into an action or condition that occurs.

1.3.n: In するようになる, it helps express a change into a new condition.

1.4.n: Connects よう to なる to indicate the condition being reached.

1.5.n: なる becomes なって, followed by きた, showing a change developing up to now.

1.6.n: Introduces the reason for the careful moisturizing described next.

2.0.n: This is the first character of 保湿, not a separate word here.

2.1.n: This is the second character of 保湿; together, the characters mean moisturizing.

2.2.n: Makes moisturizing the topic, emphasizing this part of the skincare routine.

2.3.n: Combines with に to describe the care taken when moisturizing.

2.4.n: Turns 念入り into a description of how the moisturizing is done.

2.5.n: Short for しています, a polite form describing an ongoing routine; 保湿 supplies the activity.

3.0.n: Indicates that this makeup routine happens only occasionally.

3.1.n: Refers to the face covering whose edges determine which skin remains visible.

3.2.n: Marks the mask as the boundary beyond which parts of the face extend.

3.3.n: Directly describes 部分, identifying the areas left uncovered by the mask.

3.4.n: Refers to the facial areas described by マスクからはみ出る.

3.5.n: Limits makeup application to the uncovered parts.

3.6.n: The て-form of 化粧する connects applying makeup to going to work in the next line.

4.0.n: Sets up the humorous comparison between its upper and lower halves.

4.1.n: Links 顔 to the upper and lower halves mentioned next.

4.2.n: Normally means the upper body, but here humorously refers to the upper half of the face.

4.3.n: Joins the two halves being compared.

4.4.n: Normally means the lower body, but here humorously refers to the lower half of the face.

4.5.n: Suggests the two halves look as though they belong to different individuals.

4.6.n: An informal way to express resemblance, here comparing the halves to different people.

4.7.n: Connects みたい to 色 so the comparison describes the coloring.

4.8.n: Refers to the mismatched skin tones caused by applying makeup to only part of the face.

4.9.n: Marks the appearance the speaker has when going to work.

4.10.n: Combines 出勤 with する to describe reporting for work.

4.11.n: Turns going to work this way into an event whose occasional occurrence can be stated.

4.12.n: In ことある, it expresses occasional occurrence; casual speech leaves out が after こと.

0.lit: Lately, suddenly, the cheek area—masks and things like that…
0.tip: The sentence continues into the next line; とか introduces masks as one example.

1.lit: Because makeup irritation has started to occur…
1.tip: するようになってきた describes a new condition gradually emerging up to the present.

2.lit: As for moisturizing, I am doing it thoroughly.
2.tip: してます is a conversational shortening of しています, here describing a regular habit.

3.lit: Sometimes, applying makeup only to the parts that stick out beyond the mask…
3.tip: マスクからはみ出る describes 部分 directly: the parts that extend beyond the mask.

4.lit: There are times I go to work with coloring like different people on the face’s upper and lower halves.
4.tip: 上半身 and 下半身 normally describe body halves, but here they humorously describe halves of the face.
